opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I'd be careful not to overclaim here. I don't think any meta-model is going to spit out "the next Transformer" by itself. What I hope it can do is change *how* we search for it.

Right now, architecture discovery is mostly a mix of intuition, trial and error, and a lot of compute. Someone has a hunch, they try it at small scale, and if the loss curve looks good they scale it up. The Transformer came out of that kind of process. Attention was around before, and the breakthrough was a particular combination of ingredients that happened to scale really well. But we don't have a good theory of *why* that combination works, so we can't systematically ask what the next combination should be.

My hope is that a meta-model, a model of models, gives us a more principled map of the design space. Instead of treating each architecture as a black box, you try to understand which structural properties matter for which kinds of tasks. How does information flow? What inductive biases are built in? How does the model allocate capacity across scales? If you can describe architectures along axes like these, you can start to see gaps. You can say: we've explored this region heavily, this other region is almost empty, and the theory suggests something interesting might be there.

This connects to what I've always cared about, which is doing AI research more like physics. In physics you don't just try random equations. You have principles like symmetry, conservation, and scaling, and they constrain what's plausible. I'd like architecture design to have something similar. That way the next Transformer is less a lucky accident and more something we could have partly predicted.

There's a practical side too. If a meta-model can predict from small experiments how an idea will behave at scale, the cost of exploration drops a lot. Then a small academic group with limited compute can still contribute real architectural ideas, not just big labs. To me, that democratization might matter even more than any single discovery.

So the realistic version of my hope is that it acts as a compass, not an oracle. Humans still need to bring the creativity and the taste. But the search becomes more directed, more interpretable, and hopefully a bit faster.

r001.rationale: The response says the meta-model could make the next Transformer less of a lucky accident and something researchers could have partly predicted, while clarifying it would not predict it by itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a big question, so let me start with what I mean by "meta-model," because I think the word can sound grander than what it actually is.

Right now, when we try to discover a new architecture, the process is very human. Someone has an intuition, maybe from physics, maybe from biology, maybe just from staring at failure cases for months. They try something, it works a little, they iterate, and eventually, if they are lucky and persistent, you get something like attention. The Transformer was not found by a search algorithm. It was found by people with taste. And I have a lot of respect for that, but it is slow, and it depends on a handful of people being in the right room at the right time.

What I hope a meta-model can do is make that taste a bit more explicit and a bit more shareable. The idea is to have a model that does not just learn tasks, but learns about learning. It observes how different architectural choices behave across many problems, and it starts to form a representation of what makes something work. Why does attention generalize? Why do certain inductive biases help in one regime and hurt in another? Those are questions we currently answer with folklore and ablation tables. I want them to become something a model can reason about.

So concretely, I imagine a few changes. First, the search space becomes much more interpretable. Instead of neural architecture search that produces a tangle of operations nobody can read, you get candidates that come with an explanation, something like "this component is doing a form of routing that scales well with context length." That matters to me a lot, partly because of my background in physics. I want discovery to produce understanding, not just benchmarks.

Second, I think it compresses the loop. A researcher proposes a vague idea, the meta-model turns that into several concrete variants, predicts which ones are worth training, and tells you why the others probably will not work. You still make the final call, but you waste far less compute chasing dead ends.

And third, and this is maybe the part I am most hopeful about, it lowers the barrier. The next Transformer might not come from a big lab. If a graduate student with a modest cluster can use a meta-model to explore architecture space intelligently, then the pool of people who can contribute gets much bigger.

I want to be honest about the limits, though. A meta-model will reflect the architectures it was trained on. There is a real risk it just keeps rediscovering variations of what we already have. The genuinely new thing, the next real jump, may need a kind of conceptual leap that sits outside the training distribution. So I do not see this as replacing human insight. I see it as a collaborator that handles the parts humans are bad at, like holding thousands of experiments in mind at once, so that humans can spend their time on the parts we are actually good at, which is asking the strange question nobody thought to ask.

r001.rationale: The response says the meta-model could generate architecture variants and predict which are worth training, but it does not clearly express hope that it will predict the next Transformer architecture.

astra-6.text:
My hope is that a meta-model can help us discover architectures rather than just optimize architectures we already know. Today, we make a lot of those choices by hand. We have intuitions, we try something, and then we run expensive experiments to see whether it works.

If we can turn more of those choices into something we can learn, we might explore possibilities that people wouldn’t naturally think to try. But I wouldn’t want the result to be just another complicated black box. Ideally, we could examine what the meta-model discovers and extract a simple principle that tells us why it works.

So, for me, success wouldn’t necessarily mean producing the next Transformer automatically. It would mean making the discovery process more systematic, and helping researchers find and understand ideas that would otherwise be easy to miss.

r001.rationale: The response hopes the meta-model will help researchers discover architectures and principles, but explicitly says success would not necessarily mean producing the next Transformer automatically. It does not express hope that the model will predict the next Transformer architecture.

sol-6.1.text:
My hope is that it makes the search for the next Transformer more systematic. Today, discovering a good architecture still depends a lot on human intuition and trial and error. A meta-model could help us understand why certain architectures work, identify the principles they share, and suggest new designs worth testing.

Ideally, it would do more than find a model that performs slightly better on a benchmark. It would help us develop intuitions we don’t yet have. The exciting outcome would be a feedback loop: the meta-model proposes something, we test it, and the results improve both the meta-model and our understanding.

r001.rationale: The response hopes the meta-model will identify principles and suggest new architectures to test, but it does not clearly say it will predict the next Transformer architecture.
